fransinlak: Nobody saw Norbert Fransinlak arrive. One morning there was simply one more helmet in S-F12, and a quiet sniper under it.
Norbert Fransinlak was in the first hundred. The old hands in S-F12 call them 'the early birds', and not always kindly.
Day 3. Verdel Ridge fell to the Concord. Norbert Fransinlak watched their flag go up on the heights and dug his trench a little deeper.
Norbert Fransinlak tried to dry a page near the stove. The paper survived, but the message now has the smell of toasted bread.

A clear shot from S-F12. Norbert Fransinlak gravely wounded Isidor Jackmdunn and slid back down below the parapet. A bullet went through Norbert Fransinlak's sleeve at S-F12 and took some skin with it. He kept the sleeve. Shot by Oskar Pearson of the Concord (@_william.pearson_).
Norbert Fransinlak was on light duty: bandaged, bored and in charge of the kettle.
lorenzo_sapino_: Konrad "Ash" Sapino stepped off the supply cart at S-F11 and stood very still, listening to the guns as if they were saying his name.
Konrad "Ash" Sapino is one of the first hundred to answer the call. He wears the ribbon of the First Wave.
News of the loss of Verdel Ridge reached S-F11 with the rations. Konrad "Ash" Sapino ate while listening to the revised orders.
Konrad "Ash" Sapino checked the fire step after the shelling. The wall had moved, and the spot where he always put his foot was gone.
Konrad "Ash" Sapino offered to read the newspaper aloud. The audience asked for the advertisements first, then the racing results, and the war last.
Konrad "Ash" Sapino writes everything down in a tiny notebook. Today, under fire at the Ossuary Wood, that habit was the only steady thing in S-F11.
trey15jameson: Wendel Jameson stepped off the supply cart at R-F16 and stood very still, listening to the guns as if they were saying his name.
Verdel Ridge fell to the Concord. Wendel Jameson kept the newspaper; he wanted to remember exactly what had been promised beforehand.
A shell splinter the size of a fist hit Wendel Jameson at R-F16. He is alive and he is in pain, and he needs a bed.
Wendel Jameson drifted in and out on the stretcher. Every time he woke, the line for the beds seemed longer.
Wendel Jameson lay on a stretcher under a canvas sheet and watched the orderlies carry men in and out. Nobody had time to talk.
